To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) Cu(II)-gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnR)H) complex is more effectively binding to a sheep pitutary receptor than the metal free ligand, while (b) nickel (II) and cobalt (II) are less effective than GnRH, (c) the Ni(II), Co(II) and Cu(II) complexes of GnRH are formed by co-ordination of the metal ion with four nitrogen atoms of the peptide
the binding of Cu(II) to GnRH is stronger than Ni(II) because Cu(II) can form more bonds with the peptide.

the Ni(II), Co(II) and Cu(II) complexes of GnRH are less effective in binding the sheep pituitary GnRH receptor than the metal free ligand, and the Ni(II)/GnRH complex has a rigid backbone structure in DMSO solutions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the investigation of the interaction of the GnRH peptide with metal ions and the structural analysis of these complexes.
the structural characterization of Ni(II)- and Cu(II)-gonadotropin releasing hormone complexes in solution and their binding to the sheep pituitary GnRH receptor.

the structural analysis of free and metal complexed GnRH, the binding of these complexes to a sheep receptor, and with the development of an experimental procedure to obtain high pH in a DMSO solution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Ni(II)-LHRH complexes are not able to mimic the biological activity of LHRH, while Cu(II) complexes show a good correlation with the biological activity of the free ligand.
Ni(II)- and Cu(II)-bound GnRH are both characterized by a well defined conformational state, but that the two metal ions have a different influence on the receptor binding.
the metal ions can modulate the conformation of the peptide and the binding of the peptide to the receptor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Ni(II)(GnRH)(2) complex is formed in DMSO at high pH by a mechanism which resembles that observed in aqueous solution at high pH, and that the Ni(2+) ions are co-ordinated by the peptide backbone in both cases.
the Cu(II) complex is the only one that is capable of mimicking the biological activity of the metal-free ligands.
Cu(II) is the most effective metal ion in binding to the sheep pituitary GnRH receptor, while Ni( II ) and Co(II)-GnrH are less effective.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Ni(II)(GnRH) complex is less active in receptor binding than the metal-free peptide, which can be explained by the rigid structure induced by the metal ion.

the binding of metal complexes to the receptor depends on the structure of the complexes in solution and that the structure of the complex in solution is strongly influenced by the co-ordination number of the metal ions.
metal binding to GnRH induces a rigidification of the molecule, which is in agreement with the higher binding affinity of the Cu(II) complex.
